records.title: Cell transport: follow the energy

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Explain how ATP can support glucose uptake without binding to its cotransporter.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: ATP powers the sodium–potassium pump, which maintains a low intracellular sodium concentration.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Sodium then enters through a cotransporter down its electrochemical gradient,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: providing energy for coupled glucose uptake.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: The sodium–potassium pump is inhibited in a teaching model. Why might sodium–glucose uptake weaken later?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The sodium gradient gradually becomes less able to power cotransport. The pump maintains the gradient;

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: its loss eventually reduces the energy available to secondary transport.

records.title: Three muscle types, three calcium stories

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Compare the role of calcium in skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Skeletal and cardiac muscle use troponin C to regulate actin access.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Skeletal coupling primarily releases stored calcium through voltage-sensor coupling; cardiac muscle needs trigger calcium entry.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Smooth muscle uses calcium–calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase to regulate myosin.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Why can normal skeletal muscle produce tetanic force while normal cardiac working muscle cannot?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The cardiac refractory period overlaps much of its contraction.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The long refractory period limits repeated excitation and summation into tetanus, preserving filling between beats.

records.title: Autonomic signals: receptor before response

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Give a receptor-to-response explanation of slowing at the sinoatrial node.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Acetylcholine activates cardiac M2 receptors. Gi/o signalling reduces cyclic AMP,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: while beta–gamma subunits can activate GIRK potassium channels.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: These changes reduce pacemaker activity and slow the heart.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: A learner says every sympathetic postganglionic neuron releases noradrenaline. Which example corrects the claim?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Sympathetic fibres to eccrine sweat glands release acetylcholine.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Eccrine sweat-gland innervation is the important sympathetic cholinergic exception.

records.title: The cardiac cycle: pressure opens the valves

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Predict the immediate effect of an isolated afterload increase on a pressure–volume loop.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: At unchanged preload and contractility, the ventricle must develop more pressure before ejection.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It generally ejects less on that beat,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: leaving a larger end-systolic volume and a narrower loop.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Later reflex and filling responses may modify this.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: In a simplified ventricle, end-diastolic volume is 120 mL and end-systolic volume is 50 mL.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: What is stroke volume?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: 70 mL. Subtract end-systolic from end-diastolic volume: 120 minus 50 equals 70 mL.

records.title: Ventilation: make each breath count

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Explain why rapid shallow breaths can be less efficient than slower deeper breaths at the

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: same minute ventilation.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A fixed conducting-airway volume takes up more of each small breath. After subtracting dead space,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: less fresh air reaches gas-exchanging alveoli each minute, even when total minute ventilation is unchanged.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: At the same 6 L/min minute ventilation and a fixed 150 mL dead space,

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: which pattern gives greater alveolar ventilation?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: 500 mL at 12 breaths/min. This gives (500−150)×12 = 4.2 L/min,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: because less of total ventilation is wasted in dead space.

records.title: Water balance: distinguish ADH from aldosterone

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Distinguish what ADH changes from what aldosterone changes.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability through aquaporin-2 trafficking.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Aldosterone enhances distal sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Their effects interact with medullary gradients,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: intake and circulating-volume signals.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: ADH rises, but the medullary osmotic gradient is greatly reduced. What limits water recovery?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Increased permeability still needs an osmotic driving force. ADH makes a pathway available;

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: the medullary gradient supplies the driving force.

records.title: Haemostasis: build and stabilise the plug

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Explain the difference between adhesion, aggregation and fibrin stabilisation.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Adhesion anchors platelets to an injured surface.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Aggregation joins activated platelets through fibrinogen bridges between alpha-IIb-beta-3 receptors. Coagulation generates thrombin and fibrin,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: and factor XIIIa crosslinks fibrin to stabilise the plug.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: A student confuses prothrombinase with intrinsic tenase. Which reaction belongs to prothrombinase?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Prothrombin to thrombin. Xa with Va forms prothrombinase and supports thrombin generation.

records.title: Digestion: coordinate movement and secretion

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Explain how a meal containing fat and acid can recruit different pancreatic responses.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Duodenal acid stimulates secretin and bicarbonate-rich ductal secretion.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Fat and protein products stimulate cholecystokinin and enzyme-rich secretion, with neural signals coordinating the response.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The pathways interact rather than operating as isolated switches.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Fat enters the duodenum. Which coordinated response fits its digestion?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: CCK supporting enzyme secretion and gallbladder contraction.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: CCK helps match enzyme and bile delivery to the incoming nutrient load.

records.title: Energy balance: connect intake, storage and use

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Compare nutrient handling after a meal and during fasting.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The fed state favours use and storage of absorbed nutrients under a higher insulin signal.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Fasting promotes mobilisation of stored fuels and hepatic glucose production under a lower insulin-to-glucagon signal.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Energy is transferred and transformed, not created.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Which statement best connects fasting to ongoing cellular work?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Stored substrates are mobilised to support continued metabolism.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Fasting changes fuel sources while tissues continue to use energy.

records.title: Endocrine axes: read the feedback loop

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Explain why a target-gland hormone and its pituitary signal can move in opposite directions.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: A target-gland hormone can inhibit its upstream control signals. When target-gland secretion falls,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: reduced negative feedback permits the pituitary signal to rise,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: provided the central components of the axis remain functional.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Low thyroid hormone is accompanied by a TSH that is not appropriately elevated.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: What does this challenge in a simple model?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The assumption that the central feedback response is intact.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: An intact pituitary response to primary thyroid failure would usually raise TSH;

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: central influences merit consideration.

records.title: Reproductive physiology: connect the two cycles

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Relate the ovarian and endometrial phases without assuming a fixed calendar.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Follicular estradiol supports endometrial proliferation. A sustained estradiol rise can trigger an LH surge and

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: ovulation. Luteal progesterone supports secretory endometrium; falling luteal hormones contribute to menstruation when pregnancy does

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: not maintain the corpus luteum.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: After ovulation, which hormone most directly supports secretory differentiation of the endometrium?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Progesterone from the corpus luteum. Luteal progesterone supports secretory changes following estradiol-driven proliferation.

records.title: Neural integration: from release to a response

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Distinguish chemical transmission from temporal and spatial summation.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Chemical transmission releases a transmitter that changes postsynaptic signalling or conductance.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Temporal summation combines closely timed inputs; spatial summation combines inputs at different sites.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Their combined effect helps determine whether the receiving neuron fires.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Repeated small inputs at the same synapse arrive close together and have a larger combined

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: effect. What is this?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Temporal summation. Temporal summation combines effects of closely timed inputs.

records.title: Special senses: convert a stimulus into a signal

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Compare the direction of the initial receptor response to light and to excitatory hair-bundle deflection.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Light closes cyclic-GMP-gated channels and hyperpolarises a photoreceptor.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Excitatory hair-bundle deflection opens mechanically gated channels and depolarises a hair cell.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Both graded responses regulate transmitter release.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: A hair bundle is deflected in its excitatory direction. Which initial response is expected?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Opening of mechanotransduction channels and depolarisation. Mechanical channel opening permits a depolarising current under the

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: inner-ear ionic conditions.

records.title: Microcirculation: return the filtered fluid

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Explain how venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction can both produce fluid accumulation.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Higher venous pressure can increase capillary hydrostatic pressure and filtration.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Lymphatic obstruction reduces the route that returns filtered fluid and proteins.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Both can increase interstitial fluid, but through different parts of the balance.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Two examples cause oedema: increased venous pressure and lymphatic obstruction. What differs?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: One can increase filtration; the other reduces return.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: They change different sides of the filtration–return balance.

records.title: Volume I: orient the thorax around the lung root

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Orient the two nerves at the lung root and connect one to its main motor

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: target.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The phrenic nerve runs anterior to the lung root and supplies the diaphragm through fibres

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: principally from C3–C5. The vagus runs posterior to the root and contributes to thoracic autonomic

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: networks.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: A diagram places the diaphragm low in the thorax.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Why does this not imply thoracic motor roots?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Its phrenic motor supply principally comes from C3–C5.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Adult position and developmental history must be distinguished from segmental motor supply.

records.title: Volume II: connect peritoneum and the portal triad

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Describe the portal triad while distinguishing the figure's main relationship from its simplification.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The portal vein is posterior; the bile duct and proper hepatic artery are anterior.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Conventionally the duct is right and artery left from the patient's perspective.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The figure is a front–back relationship schematic rather than a complete operative view.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: In a conventional anterior view of the portal triad,

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: where is the bile duct relative to the proper hepatic artery?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: On the patient's right. The duct conventionally lies to the patient's right of the proper

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: hepatic artery; variants exist.

records.title: Volume III: follow urine through the pelvis

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Connect the urinary route to its two renal developmental components.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Nephrons derived from metanephric mesenchyme connect to the collecting system derived from the ureteric bud.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Urine passes through collecting ducts to calyces, renal pelvis, ureter and bladder,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: then exits through the urethra.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Which developmental pairing is correct?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Ureteric bud forms the collecting system; metanephric mesenchyme forms nephrons.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Reciprocal interaction between these tissues connects nephrons to the collecting system.

records.title: Volume IV: separate taste, sensation and movement

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Explain why a single tongue map cannot replace a modality-specific answer.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: General sensation, taste and movement use different pathways. Most anterior general sensation uses V3,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: anterior taste uses VII, posterior sensation and taste use IX,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: and most motor supply uses XII. Circumvallate papillae and palatoglossus are important exceptions.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Which exception should accompany an anterior-versus-posterior tongue taste map?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Circumvallate papillae receive taste fibres from IX.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Circumvallate papillae lie just anterior to the terminal sulcus but have IX taste innervation.

records.title: Volume V: trace a limb nerve through the plexus

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Trace C5–T1 through the plexus and explain how the cords are named.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Ventral rami C5–T1 form upper, middle and lower trunks,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: each dividing into anterior and posterior divisions. These combine into lateral, medial and posterior cords,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: named relative to the second part of the axillary artery, and then give terminal branches.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: A diagram labels the posterior cord. Posterior relative to what?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The second part of the axillary artery.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The artery provides the conventional landmark for brachial-plexus cord names.

records.title: Epithelia: layers, shape and function

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Why does alveolar epithelium differ from esophageal epithelium?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Alveoli need a short diffusion distance and use thin squamous cells.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The esophagus resists abrasion with a nonkeratinized stratified squamous lining.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: A section has nuclei at different heights, but every cell contacts the basal lamina.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Which interpretation fits?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Pseudostratified epithelium is possible. In pseudostratified epithelium all cells contact the basal lamina,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: although not all reach the surface.

records.title: PCR, qPCR and reverse transcription

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: What does a positive no-template control suggest?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It suggests contamination or nonspecific signal and requires investigation before interpreting the samples.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It is not evidence of a true target in every specimen.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: A PCR tube lacks one of the two primers.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: What is the main consequence for the intended target?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Efficient exponential amplification of the bounded target is lost.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: The two primers define opposite ends and support amplification of both strands.

records.title: Enzyme catalysis and inhibition

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Why can adding enzyme accelerate a reaction without changing its final equilibrium?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Catalysis lowers the kinetic barrier for forward and reverse reaction paths.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: It changes how quickly equilibrium is reached,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: not the relative free energies of reactants and products.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: In a simple reversible competitive-inhibition model, what can increasing substrate concentration do?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Reduce the inhibitor's effect on the observed rate. Substrate competes for binding;

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: sufficiently high substrate can approach the same Vmax in the ideal model.

records.title: Complement pathways and their shared effectors

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Explain why activating complement and limiting complement are both necessary.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Activation labels and attacks targets and recruits responses.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Regulation limits amplification and terminal injury on host surfaces,

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: preserving useful defense without uncontrolled tissue damage.

transcript.speaker: Host
transcript.text: Why can different complement activation pathways have common downstream effects?

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: They converge on C3 activation and shared downstream components.

transcript.speaker: Guide
transcript.text: Convergence explains shared effects such as C3b-mediated opsonisation despite different triggers.
